title: The promise to the sages, kept
hookLine: the sages and the gods gather in the sky to watch one man stand in front of an army
carry: vachan: rama keeps his word, whatever it costs
last: A GOOD SIGN FOR A NEW START.

lines: THE GODS WATCH FROM THE SKY.
cards: Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and waits outside the empty hut. Valmiki says the sages, the gods and the celestial beings gather in the sky above Janasthana to watch.

Some are worried: one man against fourteen thousand. They pray for him aloud. Then dust rises on the horizon, the drums grow louder, and Khara's army comes into view, a dark mass like storm clouds rolling in.

teach.h: THE BOW BENT INTO A CIRCLE.
teach.b: Valmiki tells the battle over several chapters. Rama's arrows fly so fast that the rakshasas see only his bow, bent into a circle. Dushana leads an assault and falls.
Trishiras, the three-headed, comes next, and falls too. Then only Khara is left. He cuts Rama's bow and shatters his armor; Rama takes up another bow and goes on.
Khara tears up a tree and hurls it. Rama names what Khara has done: the sages terrorized, the hermits killed.
At last Khara falls. The text says it was over in a muhurta and a half, a little over an hour. The gods rain flowers, and Sita comes out of the cave and holds him.

teach.h: THE PROMISE TO THE SAGES, KEPT.
teach.b: Now remember the promise. Not long ago, the forest sages showed Rama the bones of murdered hermits and asked for protection, and he gave his word. Sita even asked whether that word was wise.
Today it's kept, at full cost, by one person. This is one of the things Hindus love most about Rama: his word holds.

teach.h: LIFE MAY GO, NOT A GIVEN WORD.
teach.b: Tulsidas gives it a line that's still quoted: in the house of Raghu, life may go, but a given word may not. The whole Ramayana turns on promises: Dasharatha's to Kaikeyi, Rama's to his father, Rama's to the sages.
And it's why the great Hindu rites are built on vows. At a wedding, the couple takes seven steps together around the fire, each step with its own blessing and promise, and the fire is the witness.
But one rakshasa, Valmiki says, slipped away.
His name is Akampana, and he's heading for Lanka.

how: The battle of Janasthana is told in many Ramlila performances as Rama's promise to the forest sages kept, and Tulsidas's line about the house of Raghu, life may go but not a given word, is still quoted for keeping one's word.

games.q: you gave your word to help someone. now it's going to cost far more than you thought. by Rama's example, what fits?
o: keep it, or the part of it you still can.
let it go; the situation changed, so the promise did too.
hand it to someone stronger to keep for you.
games.why: Rama promised the sages protection and kept it alone, against fourteen thousand. in the house of Raghu, life may go, but not a given word.

practice: Hindus begin a puja or a vow with a sankalpa: a short spoken intention, said once, with water held in the palm. Think of a promise you made that turned out harder than you expected.
Pick the smallest piece of it you can still keep today, and say it as your sankalpa. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, say it quietly to yourself. Then breathe, and keep it.

wordCard.voice: Muhurta. A traditional unit of time, about 48 minutes. Rama's battle takes a muhurta and a half. Families still ask a priest for an auspicious muhurta to begin a wedding.

orig.note: Sanskrit muhūrta: a traditional unit of time, about 48 minutes. the battle takes one and a half, a little over an hour.

carryVoice: Carry this: vachan, Rama keeps his word, whatever it costs. Tomorrow, the news crosses the sea to Ravana. Until tomorrow.
